kakekotoba.reading_secondary: しのぶ (植物・軒忍/しのぶ草)
kakekotoba.interaction: Shinobu-gusa (fern growing on old eaves, a conventional image of decay and neglect) is fused with the verb 忍ぶ 'to endure, to yearn secretly, to bear with longing' — the plant growing on the crumbling palace eaves becomes simultaneously the speaker's own act of enduring/longing for the past, so the eaves' physical decay and the speaker's emotional endurance are expressed in one word

bipartite.kami_theme: The old palace (momoshiki) with its decaying eaves overgrown with shinobu fern — an image of physical and institutional decline
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker's longing for the past (the age of imperial glory) exceeds even the capacity of 'shinobu' (endurance/longing) itself to contain
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku's visual image of decayed eaves overgrown with shinobu fern pivots, via the kakekotoba on しのぶ, directly into the shimo-no-ku's declaration that no amount of endurance or nostalgic longing can be 'enough' — the physical decay becomes the measure and trigger of an emotional excess that overflows the very word meant to name it

kigo.note: Shinobu-gusa (hare's-foot fern) growing on old eaves is a conventional image of a ruined or neglected dwelling and the passage of time rather than a seasonal marker tied to a specific time of year; it carries no strong seasonal association in the classical canon and functions here as an emblem of decline and nostalgia rather than as a kigo
